items.title: How it works
items.text: Conference programs are long. KubeCon has more than 500 sessions, and an IETF meeting has more than 1,000 active drafts in the tracked working groups. This site keeps the few items that matter to one reader. That reader is a product manager who works on physical datacenter networking, cloud-native networking, network security, and identity.

items.title: The pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
  F["Conference program"] --> P["Digest prompt"]
  P --> T["ToFaRev: shortlist, select, write"]
  T --> R["Pull request review"]
  R --> W["This site"]
  1. Discover. A weekly job checks each recurring conference for new editions and adds the confirmed ones to the registry.
  2. Fetch. After an event ends, a fetcher reads its published program: papers, talks, or drafts, with abstracts and links. Some sites block cloud IP addresses. For these sites, the owner runs the fetch from a laptop.
  3. Compose. The program goes into a prompt with the reader profile, guidance for the conference type, and the output rules.
  4. Write. ToFaRev runs the prompt in GitHub Actions with zai-org/GLM-5.3 on Nebius Token Factory. Large programs go through stages. First, batches of the program are shortlisted in parallel. Then the final picks are selected. Last, the digest is written from the selected items. ToFaRev reads the papers and slides that the picks link to, and gives their text to the writer. The writer can also fetch each pick's talk page.
  5. Check. Code, not the model, does the last checks. It removes any link that is not in the program and flags headings that do not match a program item. It also confirms that every tier is present.
  6. Link. Code, not the model, adds a row of links to every pick: the abstract page, the paper, the slides and the recording. They come from the program and the talk's own page. A recording found by search is added only when its title, its channel and its upload date all match the talk and the event.
  7. Review and publish. ToFaRev opens a pull request with the digest. When it is merged, the digest appears here and the tracking issue closes.
  8. Refresh. Recordings and slides often appear weeks after an event. Every week, for four months after each conference, the links are checked again. New ones arrive in a small pull request; the write-ups do not change.

items.title: Reading a digest
items.text:
Tier Meaning Core Directly about datacenter and WAN networking, cloud-native networking, network security, or identity. Adjacent Relevant to the broader field: useful context, or likely to matter soon. Wildcard Two to four items outside these interests that are novel or show where the field is going. Themes The patterns across the whole program.

Each pick starts with its links: Abstract (the talk or paper page, which usually lists every material), Paper, Slides and Recording, as far as they are published. A talk recording also shows a thumbnail: click it to play the talk on the page. For IETF drafts the links are the Draft, its Slides, the Session recording of the working group meeting and the session Materials.

Each pick has the same parts. Why tells you why it is worth your time. What gives the contribution in plain terms, and How gives the mechanism. Where applicable tells you whether the work is general or specific to one organization, vendor, or deployment. A write-up marked from abstract only had no fuller source available. Links come from the program, so a pick without a link had none.

items.title: Conference status
items.text:
The Conferences page shows where each edition stands:

Status Meaning Read the digest The digest is published. Digest in progress The program is fetched, and a digest is being written or reviewed. Waiting for the program The event ended, but its program is not published yet. The fetch runs again each week. Needs a local fetch The site blocks cloud IP addresses, so the fetch must run from a laptop. Needs a manual paste Automatic fetch failed. Someone must paste the program in. Fetcher stalled Fetch failed four times. The site probably changed, and the fetcher needs a fix. Upcoming The event has not ended yet.

The source, the prompts, and every digest are in hellt/conference-digest.

items.title: AutoCon 3 (Prague) — Operator
items.text:
A network-automation operator conference. Little here is directly about DC fabrics or identity protocols, but a strong subset is: two unusually candid optical-transport automation stories, a BGP telemetry build, a large-scale datacenter Terraform migration, EVPN service migration at a global telco, and several security/identity-flavored automation sessions. The rest is a clear field-wide shift from "automate operations" toward "design-driven, durable-execution, trustworthy automation" — worth skimming for where the networking discipline is heading.

Operator May 28, 2025 – May 30, 2025 Program

items.title: From Clicks to Code: Optical Network Automation Journey at GARR
items.text:
Slides Recording

Matteo Colantonio, GARR (Italian research and education network)

  • Why: Physical-layer transport (optical circuits, transponders, ROADMs) is the least-automated part of most networks, and this is a rare honest account of why the usual automation stack fails there and what actually works. Directly relevant to anyone with DC/WAN interconnect responsibilities.
  • What: GARR's progression from Ansible/AWX and the vendor controller's northbound API to a workflow-orchestrator architecture that talks directly to optical devices, now in early production use.
  • How: Ansible handled basic transponder upgrades but collapsed on complex logic — restarting cards one-by-one and verifying service recovery required three nested YAMLs with include statements. The vendor controller API was a stripped-down version of the GUI: missing key features, and useless for circuits crossing multiple line systems (mixed-platform ROADM metro regions). The pivot: build abstract service models plus Python clients speaking the same southbound interfaces the vendor controller uses (RESTCONF, TL1 shell for ROADMs), separating intent from device-specific configuration.
  • Where applicable: GARR-specific in topology (research backbone, mixed optical platforms), but the lessons — vendor NBIs as a bottleneck, direct device control, incremental automation starting with critical services — transfer to any optical/WAN environment. The observation that optical networks' GUI-centric (not CLI-centric) history changes the automation starting point is a genuinely useful framing.

items.title: Coding for infrastructure is just coding, on how we moved from a script based model to an object oriented architecture
items.text:
Slides Recording

Antonio Balmaseda & Alberto Villegas Erce, Roche

  • Why: The second of two talks at this conference independently reaching the same conclusion about optical automation (Roche's optical network uses the same devices as ESnet and GEANT). Together they read as a mini-postmortem of Ansible-and-controller-based approaches to transport automation.
  • What: Roche Pharma's move from scattered per-engineer scripts and Ansible playbooks to an object-oriented, model/controller/view architecture built on the Workflow Orchestrator framework, expected in production by the conference date.
  • How: Abstract service models with Python clients talking directly to devices (RESTCONF, TL1 for ROADMs); hardware changes only require adding implementations via Python single-dispatch, giving clean boundaries between abstract intent and device config. Concrete results from the slides: 6000 backups in 20 minutes (down from 3 hours), and 200 devices patched unattended over a weekend with no CLI access. Massive changes now ship as a JSON file plus Jinja templates through a merge request.
  • Where applicable: Roche-specific scale (worldwide multi-vendor network, thousands of devices), but the pattern — abandon YAML-nesting for real code when logic gets complex, keep Ansible only for what it's good at (backups, compliance, OS upgrades) — is broadly applicable.

items.title: Going beyond show commands and screen scraping with BMP
items.text:
Slides Recording

Bart Dorlandt (freelance network automation engineer, Netherlands)

  • Why: Verifying that BGP announcements you configured actually propagated and passed import policy is a classic gap; most shops do it with screen scraping. BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol) is the right tool and this gives the architecture and the scaling numbers.
  • What: A production pipeline for pre- and post-policy BGP data: router → BMP collector → Kafka → consumer → database → API, replacing screen scraping of show commands for customer-facing verification.
  • How: The initial consumer managed 30 msg/sec — nowhere near enough for millions of RIB entries — and was rewritten with a pool of async Kafka producers, reaching 45,000 msg/sec. Hard lessons: every stage (collector, consumer, DB) can be crippled by too much data, so filter early, deduplicate, and decide what you actually need; peer-down notifications are the critical code path; the BMP collector implementation used was incomplete and needed patches (Kafka TLS, Docker).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable wherever BGP policy correctness needs verification (peering, DC fabrics, WAN). The pipeline is buildable from open components but the scaling numbers are one implementation's — treat 30→45k msg/sec as directional, not a benchmark.

items.title: The Road to EVPN: Automated Service Migrations
items.text:
Slides Recording

Luke Gollan, Megaport

  • Why: Migrating a live global network to EVPN with automated service cutover is squarely in the PM's EVPN/BGP and interconnect territory, and this covers the whole arc: architecture, config rollout, then customer service migration with minimal disruption.
  • What: Megaport's end-to-end story of automated EVPN deployment across a global telco network, from design through rollout to migrating production services, plus customer/support-facing migration tooling.
  • How: Object-driven database generating device configs; NETCONF operations to configure, log, and track changes; diversity zones to contain blast radius; APIs and message queuing to trigger migrations; explicit phased migration steps with rehearsed rollback; tooling to track network changes and keep business stakeholders informed. (From abstract only — no usable source text.)
  • Where applicable: Megaport-specific (global NaaS/telco topology, dense service inventory), but the checklist — rehearsed rollback, diversity zones, event-driven migration triggers, stakeholder-visible risk — is a transferable migration methodology for any EVPN or fabric migration.

items.title: An Epic Journey: Automating networks with Terraform
items.text:
Slides Recording

Eduardo Pozo

  • Why: A concrete, numbers-backed account of Terraform at datacenter scale — including where it hurts (provider bugs, plan times, state risks) — which is rare and directly useful for DC automation decisions.
  • What: Using Terraform as the primary automation tool across oil, health, and enterprise projects, including migrating a large multi-site datacenter to fully automated deployment.
  • How: The slides quantify the pain: a 500+ leaf, 4-location, 2000+ VLAN fabric; a full terraform plan against an empty APIC (Cisco ACI, ~5334 resources) took 45 minutes, cut to 19 minutes by moving data transformation (dedups via set(), key lookups, validation) out of Terraform into Python. Honest coverage of vendor provider reality: "vendors say yes yes, it just doesn't work," API bugs, 12+ month-old issues, no CRUD — and the mitigations (contribute, pressure the vendor, hybrid approach, fork the provider). Also state loss/locking, apply-can-destroy surprises driven by provider quality, and preferring pipelines straight to infrastructure over controller-mediated paths where possible.
  • Where applicable: The specific numbers are ACI/APIC-specific, but the lessons (stateful tools at DC scale, controller API limits vs. parallelism, keeping computation out of your IaC layer) apply to any large fabric automation effort.

items.title: Using a SONiC Abstraction API (for fun and profit)
items.text:
Slides Recording

Josh Saul

  • Why: SONiC fragmentation across distributions is a real operational problem for multi-vendor cloud and AI infrastructure provisioning — and AI-cluster fabric provisioning is exactly where this is biting hardest right now.
  • What: A demonstration of how traditional IaC tools can drive abstractions that generate actual device configurations across multiple SONiC platforms, instead of writing per-flavor configs.
  • How: An abstraction layer over multiple SONiC flavors, with configs pushed via gNMI and (where necessary) SNMP/CLI paths. (From abstract only — no usable source text, and it's a lightning talk, so expect a demo rather than deep architecture detail.)
  • Where applicable: Directly relevant to anyone operating or evaluating SONiC-based DC fabrics with mixed distributions/vendors; less relevant if you're on a single NOS distribution.

items.title: Pls stop exposing your... secrets
items.text:
Slides Recording

John Howard

  • Why: Hard-coded credentials and verify=False on REST calls are endemic in network automation code, and the automation toolchain itself becomes an attack surface — squarely a network-security concern for the PM.
  • What: A fast tour of HashiCorp Vault's built-in secret engines, showing a PoC instance that removes hard-coded creds from automation scripts at team scale.
  • How: Standing up a Vault PoC and using a couple of its built-in engines to centralize secrets consumed by automation pipelines, addressing both the accidental-exposure problem and the DevSecOps friction it causes. (From abstract only — lightning-talk depth.)
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable; this is a generic, adoptable pattern rather than an org-specific one. Watch for the usual caveat that Vault itself becomes Tier-0 infrastructure your automation now depends on.

items.title: Automation Transforms $70 APs into Enterprise-Grade Networks
items.text:
Slides Recording

Henry Haller, Telecom Infrastructure Project (TIP) OpenWiFi

  • Why: Under the WLAN packaging, this is one of the few sessions about device identity at fleet scale — per-device certificate generation, CA signing, and mutual TLS between controller and devices, i.e., the bootstrapping problem familiar from SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity, applied to hardware.
  • What: An open-source lifecycle system (TIP OpenWiFi) that takes commodity $70 access points from zero-touch adoption to provisioned enterprise WLANs, covering WPA⅔, PSK/mPSK-RADIUS, OWE, GRE tunneling, and multi-band configs.
  • How: WAPs generate SSL certificates on adoption and submit them to a CA for signing; the certificates then authenticate the devices to the OpenWiFi Gateway via mutual TLS, creating a web of trust, with CA management included. Provisioning is driven by operator intent via JSON API transactions to the gateway and WebSocket transactions from gateway to APs. The source slides add operational lessons: immediate UI feedback and robust logging/error reporting matter because end-user feedback arrives late and through many layers.
  • Where applicable: The software is TIP OpenWiFi-specific, but the onboarding pattern — device-generated keys, CA signing, mTLS control channel — is the template for any commodity-hardware fleet (including cameras, sensors, and DC out-of-band gear).

items.title: Start at the Beginning; Automating Network Design
items.text:
Slides Recording

Claudia de Luna (Opening Keynote)

  • Why: This sets the thesis the rest of the conference keeps echoing: automation's next bottleneck is upstream of operations, in design. If the PM's teams produce monolithic diagrams and Word documents, this names the problem precisely.
  • What: An argument that the fixation on "source of truth" is a symptom of starting midstream; the real anchor is programmatically consumable design data — patterns, data models, structured data — from which diagrams, documentation, configurations, and build guides all derive.
  • How: Conceptual keynote, not an implementation: reframe design artifacts as structured data that everything else flows from, and spotlight existing work in that direction. (From abstract only.)
  • Where applicable: Universal framing; pairs naturally with the Design-Driven Automation and Abstraction talks below.

items.title: Building Trustworthy Network Automation, From Principles to Practice
items.text:
Slides Recording

Damien Garros

  • Why: The trust problem is why automation adoption stalls — teams don't delegate critical network operations to systems whose failure behavior they can't predict. This is the cleanest principles-to-patterns treatment at the conference.
  • What: A framework of design principles that make automation trustworthy, explicitly "built on mistakes, refined by experience": idempotency, dry-run, transactional commit/rollback, declarative over imperative workflows, version control, and testing.
  • How: The slides include a useful comparison table: imperative workflows make idempotency, dry-run, and transactionality hard; declarative makes them easy; version control gives all three nearly free. Patterns shown: dry-run before apply, diff-based changes, state verification, grouping changes so they either all commit or all roll back, plus process advice (enforce business process in workflows, safe defaults, "integrate what you can, build what you must").
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable, tool-agnostic; these principles map onto any automation stack (Nornir, Ansible, Terraform, orchestrators).

items.title: Transforming Network Automation with Temporal
items.text:
Slides Recording

Naveen Achyuta

  • Why: Durable-execution workflow engines are how other industries solved long-running, failure-prone, stateful orchestration — exactly what network change automation is. Temporal is underused in networking and this is a solid architectural introduction.
  • What: An introduction of Temporal to network automation: architecture, why durable execution fits network use cases (provisioning, config management, automated remediation, human-in-the-loop), and how it compares to what teams hand-roll today.
  • How: Tasks are ordinary code ("activities") whose state is persisted by the Temporal service (history service shards, matching service task queues, distributed workers) — workflows are guaranteed to run to completion, resuming where they left off after failures, with built-in tracing and audit trails. The slides show a practical trigger path (NetBox webhook → workflow) and per-step timing for optimization, plus a GitHub starter repo. Explicit caveat given: don't use it for simple tasks; it earns its keep at scale and resiliency requirements.
  • Where applicable: General-purpose; the main adoption constraint is running another stateful service well, which small teams may find heavy.

items.title: Mastering Network Operations: The Power of Abstraction
items.text:
Slides Recording

Jaakko Rautanen

  • Why: The concrete "how do I actually build abstract services" talk the design-first theme needs — with a working production stack, an open-sourced plugin, and a demo that goes from three inputs to deployed MPLS L3VPN service.
  • What: A layered automation stack in which NetBox-native data is detailed state, and a new top layer of "abstract services" (NetBox plugins) collapses daily operations to a handful of variables per service.
  • How: An example "Virtual Network" service (VRF + customer MPLS-site attachments) needs dozens of correctly-allocated details (prefixes, VLANs, loopbacks, route-targets, ASNs); the abstract model reduces user input to name, template, and site attachment, with all other values allocated automatically from template-defined ranges. Config delivery uses NetBox Config Templates (Jinja), deployment varies by vendor, and a diff view against live state precedes a one-click push. The team open-sourced the Ninja NetBox plugin for generating interactive diagrams or any text output from Jinja. Lessons: purge arbitrary encoding rules from IP/VLAN schemes, go declarative (they replace entire device configs each push), keep models generic with templates.
  • Where applicable: The implementation is a media-network MPLS/VPN environment, but the pattern (service abstraction layer over NetBox, template-driven allocation, full-config declarative pushes) is directly adoptable by anyone already running NetBox.

items.title: The Why, What, and How about Design-Driven Automation
items.text:
Slides Recording

Christian Adell Querol, Network to Code

  • Why: The most concrete instantiation of the keynote's thesis: treat design as executable, versioned, decommissionable data rather than documentation. Includes a working open-source implementation.
  • What: A framework where a network service catalog (minimal validated inputs + template logic + external context) drives a PLAN, a builder creates tracked/connected/rollbackable data, and that service data becomes the single reference for orchestration, automation (Nornir/Ansible/Terraform engines), and observability.
  • How: Demonstrated with Nautobot's Design Builder (which the speaker contributes to): a PoP deployment created from just name + size with architectural validation; a second design creating a VRF, prefix from a pool, and a cable; design updates that understand what changes (prefix preserved, cable re-pointed); clean decommissioning reverting created objects; and every change tracked as a commit. Key argument: test the design, not just the implementation — if the design is deterministic, deployments don't need per-instance review, the way nobody reviews a PR when someone launches a VPC.
  • Where applicable: The demo is Nautobot-specific, but the concepts (minimal input, design-as-data, traceable provenance, dry-run, full lifecycle through decommission) port to other SoT platforms. Speaker is vendor-affiliated (Network to Code) yet the talk is substantially technique-first.

items.title: Taking Automation to next level: Drive your network with Microservices
items.text:
Slides Recording

Shirish Basant Rai, Colt Technology

  • Why: Colt is a real carrier doing event-driven microservices for network automation aligned to TMF ODA NaaS standards — a useful signal of where operator automation architectures (and NaaS standardization) are heading.
  • What: Colt's evolution from a simple workflow-engine architecture to an event-driven microservices model, and how that architecture naturally aligned with TMF ODA NaaS.
  • How: Separation of concerns into microservices, asynchronous workflow and service-orchestration complexity hidden from consumers, code promotion without service disruption, and faster development cycles. (From abstract only — no usable source text, so expect architecture philosophy rather than deployment detail.)
  • Where applicable: Colt-specific scale (global carrier, NaaS ambitions); the microservices event-driven pattern is heavy machinery for smaller estates, but the TMF ODA alignment angle matters to anyone selling or consuming NaaS-style interconnect.

items.title: A Marathon and Not a Sprint: Lessons Learnt from Trying (and sometimes succeeding!) to Automate Enterprise Campus Networks
items.text:
Slides Recording

Robert Mertling-Blake, AEG (entertainment venues worldwide)

  • Why: An unusually honest "we are not fully automated and here's why" operator story — the failure-mode content the operator-program criteria ask for, with lessons that transfer even to non-campus environments.
  • What: AEG's journey automating campus networks across 100+ venues (>800 switches, thousands of APs), including the drivers, failures, and what finally worked.
  • How: Key lessons from the slides: assurance matters more than self-healing when the event must work (their golden rule); DCIM cable documentation at remote/unmanned sites dramatically improved remote-hands resolution; "source of record" framing gets buy-in where "source of truth" evangelism doesn't; doing automation perfectly became the enemy of doing any automation (a rushed greenfield deployment without physical connectivity or PNP time); buy the SoR-driven process wins — NetBox-driven config generation, Oxidized backups, monitoring and DDI creation that manual SOPs always missed. They deliberately keep DDI changes non-event-driven while tooling confidence grows, and deploy sacrificial old kit during construction to eat the dust.
  • Where applicable: Campus/venue-specific in details, but the meta-lessons (pick fewer battles, alignment with site refreshes, data quality as the persistent constraint) transfer to any heterogeneous multi-site estate.

items.title: Teaching "old" LLMs new tricks
items.text:
Slides Recording

Urs Baumann

  • Why: Not about networking per se, but a signal of where network automation tooling is heading: specialized models fine-tuned for automation tasks. Worth a look even for a skeptic of LLM-for-netops.
  • What: A method for making general-purpose LLMs accurate on specialized network automation tasks without datacenter-scale training budgets, plus a practical fine-tuning pipeline.
  • How: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning — adding small trainable weight matrices to a frozen base model — which sharply reduces the compute needed to specialize an LLM, applied to network-automation tasks. (From abstract only — the slide text didn't extract.)
  • Where applicable: The technique is general; the constraint is having a task set worth fine-tuning for and the discipline to evaluate accuracy claims honestly. Interesting more as a direction than a deployable today.

items.title: Network Event Correlation. Stories to keep you awake
items.text:
Slides Recording

Javier Antich

  • Why: A refreshingly blunt "why event correlation mostly doesn't work" talk, with a taxonomy of where rules end and ML/neuro-symbolic approaches begin — relevant to anyone drowning in NOC alert noise.
  • What: An honest dissection of operational noise-reduction approaches — what correlation can and cannot do today, war stories, and a proposal for doing better.
  • How: The slides frame correlation as static rules (e.g., link_down + OSPF_Down on same device/interface → correlated) over normalized inventory data, and lay out a two-column map of automation vs. autonomy across operations: static thresholds → ML goal-deviation tracking, rules-based correlation → neuro-symbolic AI, rules-based closed-loop and compliance → goal-driven autonomous agents.
  • Where applicable: Tool-agnostic and broadly relevant; the AI/autonomy roadmap is a vendor-independent framework, though the neuro-symbolic claims are forward-looking rather than shipped.

items.title: Themes
items.text:
• Design is the new frontier: The opening keynote, the abstraction talk, and Design-Driven Automation all argue the same thing — the next unlock is programmatically consumable design data (patterns, models, templates) upstream of operations, not better ops tooling. "Source of truth" is being reframed as "source of record" derived from design.
  • The Ansible/controller ceiling, twice over: GARR and Roche hit independently identical walls (no idempotent modules, YAML-nesting for complex logic, vendor NBIs missing features) and converged on the same answer: real code, abstract service models, and direct device protocols (RESTCONF/TL1). The packet world's playbook is being rewritten for optical.
  • Durable execution enters networking: Temporal, event-driven microservices at Colt, and workflow orchestrators at two research/pharma networks point to workflow-engine state management replacing fragile home-grown orchestration.
  • Trustworthiness as an engineering discipline: Idempotency, dry-run, transactional rollback, and declarative models presented as a comparable decision matrix (declarative makes all of them easy) — adoption framed as a trust problem, not a tooling problem.
  • Identity and security are quietly infiltrating network automation: mTLS device onboarding with per-device certificates in TIP OpenWiFi, Vault for automation secrets, and BMP-based verification of BGP policy — automated fleets are becoming PKI- and secrets-managed systems whether or not teams planned for it.
  • AI is present but early: LLM fine-tuning via LoRA and neuro-symbolic event correlation are directionally interesting; both talks are honest that these are pipelines and proposals rather than proven practice.

About this digest

ToFaRev picked and wrote this digest on Nebius Token Factory, from the conference's published program. A person reviewed it in a pull request before it was published. Write-ups marked "from abstract only" had no fuller source to read. Source: digests/autocon-3.md · prompt: prompts/autocon-3.md

items.title: AutoCon 4 (Austin) — Operator
items.text:
An operator-focused network automation program. Note up front: this cycle is heavy on automation practice, Day-2 operations, and the first wave of agentic-AI-in-production stories — lighter on the deep datapath/optics/identity material than a SIGCOMM or OSNA program, but the DC-fabric and WAN operator case studies below are directly on-target.

Operator November 19, 2025 – November 21, 2025 Program

items.title: Spectron: network orchestration in practice at scale; what works, what hurts
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Katarzyna Kurowska & Aldrin Isaac — eBay (Senior Software Engineer; Director, Site Network Engineering & Security)

  • Why: The single most relevant talk for physical DC fabric work: how a hyperscale-adjacent operator designs, provisions, and validates diverse DC topologies with an in-house intent-based system — including a candid "what hurts" section, which is rarer and more useful than the wins.
  • What: Spectron is eBay's spec-driven, intent-based fabric orchestration covering the ZTP lifecycle: fabric planning, spec generation, rack/TOR power-on, and deployment. Engineers write JSON topology specs (site, IP spec, node/interface specs for spines/leaves); the system renders device config, validates against a digital twin, and deploys. Multi-vendor, with explicit SONiC support. The "what hurts" half is the real value: abstractions that came out too generic or too limiting, prototypes that silently became production code, and SONiC's promise of a unified software stack across interchangeable hardware colliding with per-vendor functionality and API discrepancies.
  • How: Layered, composable abstractions — Layout (NodeSpec + InterfaceSpec), IP addressing (IPSpec + IPAllocationSpec), routing (RoutingSpec), and fungible hardware via PlatformSpec + NodeProfile — with rendering decoupled from generation and renderers composed from reusable blocks. GNS3-based topology emulation verifies before production deploy. A custom schema language and model generator keep it extensible; an adapter principle absorbs multi-vendor SONiC differences.
  • Where applicable: eBay-specific build, but the architecture lessons (define your domain early, design around primitives, embed NetEng in the dev cycle, early verification at every lifecycle stage) transfer to any operator building or buying fabric automation. Future work listed: EVPN/VXLAN overlay, test/Day-2 framework, traffic filters, HA/scalability — worth tracking if you have adjacency with the team.

items.title: Kubernetes Network Emulation, a standard interface to design and validate networks
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX)

Manodipto Ghose & Ryan Elliott (no affiliation given in program)

  • Why: Sits exactly at the intersection of the PM's cloud-native and physical-network interests: it uses Kubernetes as the substrate for emulating real multi-vendor network OSes, enabling shift-left validation without lab hardware.
  • What: KNE (openconfig/KNE) is a vendor-neutral network device emulation framework: containerized vendor NOS images wired into arbitrary topologies on Kubernetes, with lifecycle management provided by k8s. Paired with the OpenConfig Feature Profiles repo and the ONDATRA test framework, it enables "write test once, run anywhere" — the same tests against a virtual KNE testbed and a physical one. Claimed outcomes: weeks/months saved over waiting for testbed procurement, and at least 50% savings in testbed build costs.
  • How: Topology defined as nodes (vendor NOS containers, e.g. Arista cEOS, with bootstrap config and certs) plus A-to-Z links; Ixia-c (containerized Open Traffic Generator, OTG model-based API with Snappir/GoSnappi SDKs) injects traffic and emulates control planes (e.g. BGP peers) at points in the topology. OTG scales from containers to hardware generators via the same API.
  • Where applicable: Open-source and broadly applicable, with one hard dependency: your NOS must have a container image (major vendors do). Best fit for feature/compliance testing and CI; not a performance- or optics-fidelity tool — control-plane and functional behavior only. The "compliance as code" angle (shared test suites in featureprofiles) is a genuine standardization play worth watching.

items.title: Overhauling Data Center Network Automation: Intel's Data-Centric Journey
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Greg Botts — Intel (Senior Network Engineer)

  • Why: A rare full-journey DC automation case study at real scale (global, 5k+ devices, new network platform + new automation system simultaneously), with a clear architectural position: data first, everything else is a by-product.
  • What: Intel IT replaced a turnkey vendor automation solution (inflection point: roadmap, scale, and cost limits) with a data-centric system built on Nautobot as the network source of truth, plus open-source components, DBaaS, and config generation. Timelines are concrete: 6-month prototype, 8-month pilot, 1-year migrations — delivered on time and under budget. Results: provisioning time reduced ~75%, 100% standardized configs.
  • How: Foundation is modeled, centralized, programmatically accessible network data (device inventory, device data, jobs, golden config → intended config). Key learnings: model for scale, right-size and enable log-cleaner (hosting matters), and "relentlessly standardize" — eliminate one-offs. The modeled data is explicitly positioned as the on-ramp for AI ("table is set for AI") and self-service for partners and customers.
  • Where applicable: Intel-internal, but the methodology (data-first, NSoT as foundation, staged rollout) is general and vendor-neutral — Nautobot is open source. Most useful if you run a large multi-site DC estate and are weighing build-vs-buy on automation; the talk includes their actual build/buy criteria list.

items.title: ESnet's new Micro-Service based Discovery Service
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Marc Koerner — ESnet

  • Why: ESnet operates a national science WAN with optical line systems — the closest thing in this program to the PM's DC/WAN interconnect and optics interests. This is a production (since June 2025) redesign of how bulk network data is collected and normalized, born from real operational pain.
  • What: A Kafka-based, notification-driven discovery and document-repository architecture replacing per-application polling. Previously, multiple tools independently queried devices for overlapping purposes (optical circuit sync with the config DB, L2/L3 topology for the OSCARS L2VPN tool), causing redundant collection, inconsistent data across apps, and unnecessary device/network load. The Discovery Service centralizes this into one low-friction mechanism with pluggable normalizers.
  • How: Agent Controller (scheduler, dedup of discovery requests) distributes work via Kafka to Discovery Agents, which pull data from sources — NETCONF from devices, RESTCONF from the TNMS management system, or even spreadsheets. Documents (up to 80MB, compressed) land in the "Andy Lake Service" repository with metadata and history; stacked/parallel normalizers (implementing the TOWL equipment ontology) generate normalized views and compute change notifications. Fine-grained controls: configurable audit intervals, namespace-level gets, regex filters to strip counters and sensitive data before storage. Deployed as microservices on Kubernetes (two prod clusters plus staging) with GitLab/Argo CD/Rancher.
  • Where applicable: ESnet-specific stack (Kafka, TOWL, k8s), but the design pattern — notification-driven bulk data management with normalized views — generalizes to any multi-tool operator drowning in redundant polling. The honesty about equipment is valuable: vendor NETCONF/YANG standard violations, devices that lock up under discovery, models so large the device times out, and NSO being slow at non-config retrieval. Budget for these if you attempt the same.

items.title: Scaling Network Operations with Modular Ansible: A Multi-Environment Automation Framework
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Joseph Nicholson — NTT DATA, Global IP Network (AS2914)

  • Why: A Tier-1 transit backbone operator's playbook for scaling Ansible across a multi-vendor WAN including DWDM — backbone routers across three vendors, optical across two — which matches the PM's WAN and interconnect focus.
  • What: Six years of evolving an Ansible repository into a modular, multi-environment automation framework serving GIN's 800+ network elements (250+ backbone routers, 100+ DWDM elements across 5 continents, 40+ countries, 90+ PoPs), covering software upgrades, maintenance snapshots, traffic updates, and circuit testing — run from CLI and AWX.
  • How: Dynamic inventory is a Python script pulling all device data (platform, vendor, OS, location, monitoring status) from GUMS, their in-house change-management system with 25+ years of lineage (started as Verio tooling in the late 1990s) — groups are built per vendor/platform/device-type on every playbook run. CI/CD pipeline gates merges on #FIXME tags and syncs revision vars to AWX hourly; task files are shared across playbooks with a careful include (dynamic) vs import (static) discipline; folder structure is per-playbook, subdivided per NOS.
  • Where applicable: NTT GIN-specific in its dependence on GUMS and org history, but the transferable lessons are explicit: adopt pipeline and AWX APIs earlier, enforce repository naming policy, use dynamic inventory from your existing change system rather than maintaining static files, and understand include/import semantics before sharing task files. Honest about the trade-off: shared task files update many playbooks at once — and break many at once.

items.title: From Band-Aids to Best Practices: USAA's Network Automation Journey
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Brandon Cavett — USAA (Senior Infrastructure Engineer)

  • Why: A concrete, Arista-centric DC story of the pattern most enterprises actually live: Day-1 rack provisioning automated early, Day-2 becoming the real problem, and config-as-code (AVD) as the resolution — including retrofit difficulty and engineer-training costs.
  • What: USAA built end-to-end automated rack provisioning (CloudVision config builders via API, switch provisioning in under an hour hands-off), then hit Day-2 reality: CLI-first changes, drift between designed and running config in CloudVision when standalone Ansible playbooks pushed directly to switches, and heavy per-playbook testing. They adopted Arista AVD (Architect, Validate, Deploy), which standardized config fabric-wide, enabled sweeping changes quickly, and let them use CloudVision's change-control process to pre-stage and review changes. Most recent environments are 100% config-as-code; the Day-1 provisioning pipeline was replaced by AVD entirely.
  • How: AVD (Ansible collection) generates config from structured intent and deploys via eAPI or CloudVision; pre-provisioning pipelines export the data needed to add new switches into AVD. Next steps: wrap the whole process in CI/CD with Arista Cloud Test (ACT) for pre-deployment testing and ANTA for post-validation, plus retrofitting legacy environments.
  • Where applicable: USAA/Arista-specific (AVD, CloudVision, ACT/ANTA are Arista tooling), so directly applicable only to EOS/CVP estates — but the drift problem from out-of-band playbook changes, the change-control-integration pattern, and the "training traditional network engineers on Git/CI/Ansible is the hard part" observation generalize broadly.

items.title: The Secret to Network Config & Security Compliance at Scale
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Vincent Phelan — Head of Network Architecture & Automation (financial sector)

  • Why: The PM's network-security interest gets its strongest entry here: a working, scaled config-compliance system at a bank, with real numbers, built on open components (OPA, TextFSM, GitOps) rather than a compliance product.
  • What: A config/security compliance pipeline that runs compliance for 7,000 devices against 70 policies in about one minute, treating architecture (constraints, standardization, cutting the product count) and automation as one discipline rather than two teams. Includes five anti-patterns from 20 years of war stories — premature optimization, snowflake-tolerant design, manual data massaging, imaginary scaling fears, and forcing formats (YAML/Jinja2) on engineers who don't natively speak them.
  • How: Collect generic data from any source via device command output, parse with TextFSM ("yet to find something more generic and not AI"), filter junk before processing, and keep everything with a "not yet" adage. Compliance rules are expressed as Open Policy Agent (Rego) policies — and, in the "write programs that write programs" spirit, the OPA policies themselves are auto-generated with expected/actual/allow fields and control-mapping metadata (control ID, description) baked into each evaluation, producing per-device, per-control, per-evaluation overviews. The GitOps repo scales to 3.5M objects / ~20GB. Drift detection and remediation close the loop.
  • Where applicable: Technique is org-agnostic and built on open source; the control-mapping metadata pattern is especially transferable to any regulated environment (financial, healthcare) where compliance evidence must tie to specific controls. The architecture-first stance (reduce product count before automating) is a prerequisite, not an option — the speaker is explicit that automation bolted onto a patchwork fails.

items.title: Is MCP just an API Abstraction?
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

William Collins — Director, Technical Evangelism

  • Why: MCP is the emerging protocol substrate for agentic systems interacting with infrastructure — directly relevant to the PM's workload/agentic identity and protocol interests (how agents authenticate, discover capabilities, and get scoped access is the same problem class as OAuth/OIDC/SPIFFE, one layer up). This is the sharpest protocol-level dissection in the program.
  • What: A point-by-point architectural comparison of MCP against REST APIs, concluding MCP is not merely an API wrapper: REST is stateless, URL-routed, and built for human developers; MCP is a stateful, session-based JSON-RPC protocol with dynamic capability discovery, built for AI models to interact with external systems safely. The framing of the N×M integration problem (N models × M tools = N×M custom integrations, with quadratic maintenance and vendor lock-in) collapsing to N+M (N clients + M servers) is the clearest articulation of why the protocol matters.
  • How: MCP's three primitives — Resources (read data/context), Prompts (templates), Tools (execute actions) — plus context (semantically-tagged data loaded into the model's window) and logs (diagnostics pushed back). Decorators auto-generate tool schemas from docstrings, eliminating the glue code and agent-loop plumbing of hand-rolled function calling. The talk's best design guidance is intention-based tool design (run_compliance_check(device_group, policy) rather than endpoint-mapped getters), role-based capability filtering via tags to prevent decision paralysis, and MCP gateway patterns as evolution paths. It also cleanly separates intelligence (understanding intent) from scale (concurrency, multi-tenancy).
  • Where applicable: Protocol-general, vendor-neutral, with working code (github.com/wcollins/talks). Caveat: the speaker is a technical evangelist, but the content is architecture analysis, not a product pitch. Directly applicable to anyone designing agent-to-infrastructure access — and the role-based tool-exposure idea is effectively least-privilege scoping for agents, a live question in agentic identity.

items.title: From Manual to Marathon: My Automation Journey at HEB
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Erich Crosswhite — H-E-B

  • Why: The best near-miss postmortem in the program: a change that nearly removed DNS servers from the production config chain, what guardrail failed, and how the pipeline was hardened afterward.
  • What: An IaC journey for a new Arista environment at a 400+ store retailer: AVD-based config generation, GitLab MRs with peer review, AWX webhooks, CloudVision (CVaaS) change controls, auto-generated Confluence docs, and — after the near-miss — Nautobot integration for access-port config that was subsequently removed, not because the product failed, but because the author's scripting lacked controls.
  • How: The DNS incident: a Nautobot data cleanup (logical cables disconnected) propagated through CI/CD and the generated config dropped DNS servers; luck (execute_tasks: false in CloudVision) prevented an outage. The fix: build stage generating config from both main and feature branches, a validate stage diffing them plus Batfish verification, results reported directly into the merge request for review before deploy. Also includes a lab cautionary tale (a state: absent that wiped the lab fabric to ZTP) and future work toward Container Lab digital twins with ANTA validation.
  • Where applicable: H-E-B/enterprise-specific and Arista-stack-specific, but the pipeline design (MR-integrated diff + Batfish gates, guardrails around SoT-driven generation) is adoptable by anyone. The core lesson — the SoT product was fine; the unguarded integration was the risk — generalizes completely.

items.title: Toward Autonomy
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Scott Robohn — NAF | Solutional

  • Why: The best framing talk of the cycle for where closed-loop network operations is heading — useful context for any PM whose roadmap touches autonomous remediation.
  • What: "Control Plane 3.0": autonomy as a continuum (scripted automation → goal-driven adaptive behavior), not a feature you turn on. Argues we already run autonomous systems — BGP being the exemplary model (distributed, convergent, bounded impact) — and enumerates the necessary ingredients: control loops fed by telemetry, fail-safe error handling for states you didn't anticipate, incremental workflow-by-workflow development, and people and trust built through measurable experiments and gated rollouts.
  • How: Phased rollout per use case (experiment → PoC → limited prod → scale), with a difficulty tiering that rings true (easy: device OS upgrade, branch CPE turn-up; medium: SP edge turn-up, multi-tenant segmentation; hard: global failover orchestration, brownout mitigation, intent-drift remediation). AI is positioned as a "how, not a what" — one tool among several, with hybrids of AI and traditional mechanisms called the most likely effective path. Reference scaffolds: TM Forum autonomy models, ETSI ENI, IBN — "models as scaffolding, not doctrine."
  • Where applicable: Conceptual rather than a case study, but the difficulty tiers and cross-domain orchestration framing (LAN + DC + WAN + cloud + security, and IP/optical alignment as an opportunity) are directly relevant to DC/WAN planning. No org-specific dependencies.

items.title: 2025 State of Network Automation Survey Results
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Chris Grundemann — Network Automation Forum

  • Why: Field-wide data every PM in this space should have on hand: 681 responses (352 complete) across 58 countries and 34 industries — an order of magnitude larger than prior years (106 in 2024, 78 in 2023).
  • What: The headline findings paint a less rosy picture than conference hallways suggest. Mean self-assessed automation is 37.5% (down from ~42% the prior two years — plausibly a sampling effect from more early-stage and enterprise respondents), 73% of orgs are at or below 50% automated. The "half-nots": half of organizations have less than 30% automation, no LLM plans (only 3% have LLMs deployed with production network access; ~45% have no plans), zero dedicated automation staff, don't measure automation success, and are misaligned with leadership. 44% of reported barriers are "people" problems (skills 27%, organizational 20%, cultural 14%); technical is only 10%.
  • How: Survey methodology with year-over-year comparability caveats the presenter himself flags ("Caveat Emptor" — sample composition shifted notably: 39% USA vs 58% in 2023, enterprise share up to 42%). Tooling data: 82% homebrew, Ansible dominates OSS (53%), Python at 93% of scripting; top automated tasks are backups and device deployment; the largest gaps between current and desired automation are troubleshooting (+223), capacity planning (+167), and traffic engineering (+156).
  • Where applicable: Globally sourced and broadly indicative rather than statistically pure — use the directional findings (people barriers, the troubleshooting gap, minimal production AI) to calibrate roadmap assumptions, not as precise benchmarks.

items.title: HAWAT: An AI Assistant for Network Troubleshooting
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Karl Newell & Matt Mullins — Internet2

  • Why: A working agentic AI assistant interfacing directly with network hardware at a national research network — one of the few demos in the program where an LLM-driven agent reasons through real protocol failure modes.
  • What: HAWAT (Heuristic Analysis With Adaptive Troubleshooting): an agentic chatbot that interprets network conditions and executes commands on infrastructure. Demonstrated on both a lab topology and Internet2's 88-device production-scale national network (aggregation routers, core routers, global exchange points), including live latency tests (NY–LA, ~69ms) and BGP route-origin analysis per neighbor/VRF.
  • How: LLM + RAG (over network documentation) + ReAct agentic framework. The demos shown are the convincing kind: diagnosing an OSPF adjacency failure to a hello-interval mismatch (10s vs 20s) with the specific log lines, explaining adjacency flapping from "inactivity timer expired" / "nbr did not list our router ID", and drawing ASCII topology with data-plane vs management-plane distinction. Next steps are MCP and agent-to-agent protocols.
  • Where applicable: Internet2 research-network context, and the demos include pre-recorded sessions — evaluate the failure-diagnosis patterns rather than production readiness. The approach (LLM as reasoning front-end over a bounded command set, with RAG grounding in topology and docs) is replicable in any environment; the risk profile of letting it execute commands is yours to scope.

items.title: The NetDevOps Journey: Manual Firefighting to Agentic Autonomy
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Greg Freeman — Lumen (VP Network & Customer Transformation) — Closing Keynote

  • Why: Scale and candor from one of the world's largest networks — ~340,000 fiber route miles, 350+ Tbps backbone, AS1 — on both what large-scale automation achieved and a sober reading of AI's failure statistics.
  • What: Lumen's operational transformation: 80% "hands out of the network" via machine-to-machine communication, 350+ workflows developed, running at a pace of ~10 workflows per minute 24×7, built on Itential orchestration with an integration layer spanning ticketing, alarming (Splunk, RFM), CMDB, and dozens of system adapters. The second half pivots to AI: an MCP architecture with an MCP service layer (Ollama in DDC, Databricks/Claude) exposing internal tools to agents, plus a "Supervisor Agent" above them — and an AI use case for pinpointing fiber-cut GPS locations.
  • How: The automation strategy is standards-plus-process ("no shortcuts": PDDs, SDDs, training, "upscaling employees" rather than replacing them). The AI section is notable for citing both Wharton's optimistic outlook and MIT's cautionary one (of $30–40B invested in custom AI projects, ~95% see zero return; organizational readiness, not technology, is the limiter), plus clear "what AI is not" caveats: non-deterministic outputs need human oversight, it is not a universal replacement, and it requires continual upkeep.
  • Where applicable: Lumen-specific scale and Itential-based stack — the workflow counts and mediation architecture are their topology. Transferable: the tiered support-culture shift, the supervisor-agent-over-MCP-services pattern, and the discipline of treating AI adoption as an organizational-readiness problem. Treat the ROI claims as directional; the cited MIT/Wharton tension is the honest part.

items.title: From CLI to Model: Building a Foundational Source of Truth for Brownfield Networks
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Munachimso Nwaiwu — Revelo (open-source project)

  • Why: Addresses the barrier that stops most brownfield automation: no source of truth on a legacy network with no budget — with an open-source methodology and working code rather than advice.
  • What: A three-step pipeline ("Revelo"): bootstrap an inventory (either explicit IP/credentials/platform, or discovered via nmap -O including hidden subnet devices), build a structured SOT by parsing live state into JSON, and validate state with automated diffs. Demonstrated on a multi-vendor lab (Cisco IOS/IOS-XE/NX-OS, Junos).
  • How: NAPALM for vendor-neutral getters (facts, interfaces IPs, LLDP neighbors), Netmiko as the "truck" for CLI commands NAPALM doesn't cover, and Genie (pyATS) as the parser. The versioning design is the clever part: inventory/1/, sot/1_2/ (snapshot 2 under inventory 1), diff/1_2/ — producing an auditable history and two validation modes: live compliance ("is the network compliant right now?") and offline audit ("what changed last night?") with clean structured diffs instead of config noise.
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to any brownfield network with programmatic CLI/API access — no greenfield or budget required, and the components are all mainstream open source. Limits: it captures operational state as the baseline, so your "intended state" is initially defined by whatever is actually running — a starting point, not a governance model.

items.title: Bridging Infrastructure and Data
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Marco Martinez — Swisscom (Infrastructure Automation Architect)

  • Why: An IPAM-relevant engineering talk: dynamic, SoT-driven resource allocation (e.g. "give me an unused IP") pushed directly into Terraform, solving the impedance mismatch between dynamic schemas and static provider definitions.
  • What: A proof-of-concept custom Terraform provider for Infrahub, powered by GraphQL, that eliminates static .tfvars files and makes infrastructure data (unused IPs, standard vSwitch configs, cloud-provider IP reservations) directly available — read-only and read-write — inside IaC workflows, with an automated pipeline that builds and publishes the provider.
  • How: The core problem is that Infrahub has a dynamic schema (no default schema; it changes per instance and branch) while Terraform providers expect static schemas in Go — and no Go SDK existed for Infrahub. The solution: a generator that takes your GraphQL queries, uses genqlient to produce a typed Go SDK, and templates a provider from them — schema baked in per version, published to a private registry, make all to build. Documented honestly: the design choices brought significant complexity, and self-built providers are not the norm.
  • Where applicable: PoC-stage and Swisscom-context; the pattern (dynamically generating a provider from queries rather than hand-maintaining one) generalizes to any GraphQL-backed SoT/IPAM system (Infrahub, or similar). Directly relevant to anyone who wants IPAM allocation to happen inside Terraform plans instead of spreadsheets.

items.title: A Harmonized, Standards-based Ontology for Telco-grade Agents
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Dave Duggal — EnterpriseWeb (founder/CEO)

  • Why: Not a fit for the PM's core stack, but it is the most idea-dense 30 minutes in the program: a serious architectural argument for why LLM agents can't be telco-grade without formal knowledge engineering — and a critique of the industry's current GraphRAG/RAG direction.
  • What: The argument: statistical pattern matching (GenAI/agentic AI) is not good enough for reliable, available networks — backed by cited benchmarks (best-performing models at 25% full-sequence-match accuracy on nested API-call tasks; "context rot" research; Apple's "illusion of thinking"). The proposal: knowledge graphs with formal ontologies (harmonizing 3GPP, O-RAN, TMF, ETSI NFV, TOSCA, MPLIFY LSO) as the deterministic layer, with the KG as a "control language" over language models — low-token, low-latency, energy-efficient, deterministically validating inferences — and as a secure blackboard providing shared memory, domain knowledge, temporal history, and tools to agents under strong governance.
  • How: The technical meat is a "ladder of abstraction" from relational tables through labeled-property graphs and RDF triplestores to hypergraphs supporting multi-dimensional, conditional, n-ary relationships — with pointed analysis of why each lower rung fails (joins are expensive; LPGs can't model n-ary object relationships; RDF triples explode with complexity). The KG sits behind an MCP server as "Context-as-a-Service."
  • Where applicable: Telco-centric (3GPP/TMF framing, 6G "AI-native" vision) and vendor-originated (EnterpriseWeb CEO), so discount accordingly — but the underlying critique and the hypergraph-over-RDF/LPG reasoning apply to anyone building agent governance for infrastructure where determinism matters. Pairs naturally with the PM's identity interest: this is effectively an argument for formal, governable agent context and permissions.

items.title: Battle of the Bots: Which AI Models Actually Work for Network Engineering Tasks
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Eric Chou — Network to Code

  • Why: A genuinely reusable decision framework rather than another AI demo — and the methodology (expected-value analysis plus task-specific evaluation) transfers to any AI adoption decision, including agent/identity tooling.
  • What: The premise: "which model is best?" is the wrong question; the right one is "what is the expected value of using AI for this task with this model?" A lightning talk with a decision-tree method: map decision points, calculate probabilities of success, and derive expected value per option — illustrated with a worked RCA example (AI root-cause platform at 75% success rate, 30-minute resolution vs 4-hour manual, $4k/hr downtime cost, $10k SLA penalty — EV of AI-powered RCA $11,000 vs -$26,000 for manual).
  • How: Three practical evaluation methods to establish the probability inputs: expert review (human in the loop), automated code evaluation (digital twin for pass/fail), and AI-as-judge. The takeaway: build your own evaluation system and iterate — with a sensible default (Claude) as the starting point, not the conclusion.
  • Where applicable: Task- and org-specific by construction — the whole point is that you run it on your tasks with your cost/downtime numbers. Broadly applicable wherever AI tooling is being considered for repeatable technical work; the evaluation-system pattern (expert + code + AI judge) is the durable part.

items.title: Themes
items.text:
• Data-first is the settled consensus: Intel (Nautobot NSoT as foundation), ESnet (centralized discovery + normalization), the brownfield SOT talk, and Swisscom's Infrahub integration all independently converged on "model the data first; everything else is a by-product." Source-of-truth design is where the architectural effort now goes.
  • Agentic AI crossed from demos into operator practice — but production reality is thin: HAWAT, Lumen's supervisor-agent-over-MCP architecture, and constrained-accuracy pipelines (Building AI with AI) show real systems; the survey shows only 3% of orgs with LLMs deployed against production network data and ~45% with no plans. The gap between conference content and field adoption is the widest it's been.
  • MCP specifically, not "AI" generally, is the concrete protocol story: the MCP dissection talk, Lumen's MCP service layer, HAWAT's roadmap, and the telco-ontology talk (MCP as context server) all treat MCP as the integration substrate — with intention-based tool design and role-based capability filtering emerging as the de-facto scoping model for agent access.
  • Validation shift-left went mainstream: digital twins (Spectron/GNS3, KNE, Container Lab), pre-merge config diffs with Batfish, ONDATRA "write once, run anywhere" against virtual and physical testbeds — verify-before-deploy is now assumed practice, not novelty.
  • Day-2 is the honest battleground: USAA's drift-and-retrofit story, HEB's near-miss, NTT's upgrade workflows, and the lifecycle-automation material all describe the same arc — provisioning gets automated first, then Day-2 maintainability (guardrails, change control, training) is where programs succeed or stall.
  • The constraints are organizational, not technical: the survey's 44% "people" barriers, Lumen's MIT citation (95% of custom AI projects see zero return for readiness reasons), and the leadership track's sociotechnical framing all point the same direction — skills, trust, and sponsorship, not tooling, are the rate limiters this cycle.

About this digest

ToFaRev picked and wrote this digest on Nebius Token Factory, from the conference's published program. A person reviewed it in a pull request before it was published. Write-ups marked "from abstract only" had no fuller source to read. Source: digests/autocon-4.md · prompt: prompts/autocon-4.md

items.title: AutoCon 5 (Munich) — Operator Program
items.text:
AutoCon 5 is a network-automation operator conference, so nothing here touches optics, RDMA/lossless fabrics, eBPF/Cilium, or FIDO/SPIFFE directly. The value for this PM is in the physical-fabric and WAN automation war stories (EVPN/VXLAN, SRv6 backbones, an 800G pan-European migration), one genuinely strong network-security automation case, and the agentic-AI governance debate that dominated the leadership track. Picks below are grouped accordingly.

Operator June 10, 2026 – June 12, 2026 Program

items.title: Network Operations Automation at DE-CIX
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Lucas Immanuel Nickel · Network Operations Engineer — DE-CIX

  • Why: One of the few talks treating network automation itself as production infrastructure with SRE discipline — reliable delivery, observability, safe failure — at an interconnection platform whose fabric is the product.
  • What: DE-CIX (3,700+ connected networks, 100+ routers, hundreds of circuits) runs 15+ production web services, 20+ cron jobs and 500+ executions/day from one shared library. Two shipped patterns: a gNMIc config-generation job driven from Zabbix + NetBox, and a geospatial network view service; both deploy via GitOps in under 10 minutes.
  • How: All workloads (cron jobs and web services) run in Kubernetes behind a single standardized CI/CD path (Kaniko → Harbor → Helm → K8s, Renovate for deps). The gNMIc generator turns Zabbix host/proxy and NetBox device data into proxy configs exposing device telemetry as Prometheus metrics. "Geo" correlates NetBox + Zabbix into a live geographic view, inferring relationships from imperfect data and preferring "incomplete but honest output" over silent success. 1 in 3 deploys is rejected before production — failure moved deliberately left.
  • Where applicable: The GitOps delivery and defensive-automation patterns are broadly applicable; the scale and IXP workflows (route servers, FPU fiber switching) are DE-CIX-specific. The Kubernetes investment assumes you already run a container platform for network tooling.

items.title: Rethinking Network Monitoring
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Christian Adell & David Flores · CoreWeave

  • Why: The clearest architectural statement at the conference that monitoring is the feedback signal for automation, not a dashboard problem — from a GPU-cloud operator running hyperscale DC fabrics.
  • What: The argument is that the gap isn't tooling but architecture: observability is a pipeline (collector → processor → distribution → persistence → visualization) that must be diverse (metrics, logs, flows, state, config), integrable (tied to the SoT and the orchestrator so the loop closes), and scalable (federated, cardinality-aware). The stated goal: a device added to the SoT starts being monitored automatically; a 3am interface degradation is verified and remediated by a workflow, no human.
  • How: Normalize multi-vendor telemetry (gNMI vs SNMP schemas) into a common shape; enrich with SoT context (role, location, owner, maintenance status) — but only with labels that drive decisions, since every label multiplies time series. SoT decides what gets monitored (push/webhook over periodic sync); "an alert is a contract, not a notification" — alerts must be machine-consumable by the orchestrator.
  • Where applicable: The pipeline pattern is vendor-agnostic and transfers to any fleet. The "hundreds of thousands of devices" framing is CoreWeave-scale; smaller operators can adopt the architecture without the federation complexity.

items.title: Reaching Fully Automated Backbone Networks: A Network Developer's Journey
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Eugen Serban & Bartek Bacal · Swisscom

  • Why: A production SRv6 backbone at carrier scale, with the honest four-year delta between architecture PowerPoints and reality — squarely in this PM's WAN/protocol territory.
  • What: Today: >3,000 devices (~10k target) running SRv6 orchestrated by NSO with zero manual CLI, >25k public-facing service instances (>150k target), and zero escalated major incidents. The candid part: standardization struggles, early engineering choices that hurt, toolkit woes, organizational and cultural hurdles (Dev vs Ops, Network Engineer vs Developer), and northbound processes that didn't adapt.
  • How: A virtual dev stage with repeatable testing superseded earlier tooling; automatic documentation; a deliberately small standardized service catalog (L2VPN/EVPN, L3VPN, SRv6) so each component is replaceable. Open challenges named explicitly: true CI/CD, scale testing (YANG leafrefs and "for loops" causing exponential runtime growth), and closed-loop self-healing split into awareness → analysis → decision → execution.
  • Where applicable: Swisscom-specific SP environment, NSO-centric. The org lessons (the hardest problems were not the network) and the scale-testing pitfalls transfer to any backbone automation program.

items.title: Automation at Scale Across Domains: DC, Campus, and WAN
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Christian Breunig · Network Architect — Rohde & Schwarz

  • Why: A full EVPN-VXLAN fabric program — dual DCs, campus, WAN — with a quantitative answer to "how much Day-2 work will there really be?" (much more than you think).
  • What: 500+ devices under unified Git/Ansible/GitLab CI. Change volume grew from 109 (2021) to 1,060 (2025) as the network became a service-provider-like internal backbone — the "few VLANs a year" assumption died quickly. They maintain a 100% EVE-NG replica of the network at all times and spend ~80% of their time in the QA environment.
  • How: Declarative, data-driven model: NetBox as SoT, data determines what gets rendered (VLANs on port-channels, VLAN database, VNIs). One inventory per domain (DC/LAN/WAN) with domain-specific inheritance (DC.yml/LAN.yml/WAN.yml); ANTA for post-change validation (e.g., detecting decommissioned endpoint ports); ansible-lint/yamllint enforced. Scaling tips include 2-byte vs 4-byte ASN pitfalls (the RD is only 32-bit) and careful MLAG peer-link addressing to avoid customer-VRF conflicts.
  • Where applicable: Single-vendor (Arista + AVD + CloudVision) — that's the constraint. The QA-digital-twin discipline, the change-rate data, and the MLAG/ASN gotchas transfer to any EVPN fabric program.

items.title: Ten Years of Network Automation at LINX
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Riccardo Verzeni · Director of Software Engineering — LINX

  • Why: A decade-long incremental journey at a large IXP — customer port provisioning, MAC ACL port security, rate limiting, quarantine testing, thousands of route-server BGP sessions — the physical interconnect + BGP combination this PM lives in.
  • What: Three phases: NCA (config-as-code from structured data, Jinja2/Ansible/NAPALM, reviewable diffs, git audit trails), NCA 2.0 (unsupervised, asynchronous member self-service via API → message queue → worker), and OMS-based service orchestration plus route-server automation. A bespoke SoT (TSI) was built because nothing on the market fit an IXP with a telco's workflows but not its scale — today they'd probably use NetBox.
  • How: The standout pattern is the pause–resume hybrid model: the OMS workflow pauses when external action is required (member validates config in quarantine VLAN, invited member accepts a private VLAN, NOC patches a physical port) and resumes automatically once satisfied. Explicit guardrails: locking, serialized deploys, hash-verification of pushed files, defaulting to humans for corner cases.
  • Where applicable: IXP workflows are LINX-specific, but the pause-resume pattern, the phase-by-phase trust building, and the DO/DON'T list (don't build bespoke by default; don't over-engineer error handling) are broadly transferable.

items.title: GitOps the Hard Way: Rebuilding a Source of Truth (Three Times)
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Radim Roška · ALTEPRO solutions (per slides)

  • Why: The hardest problem in EVPN fabric automation is the data model, not the tooling — demonstrated by rebuilding the schema three times before it survived production. Directly relevant DC-fabric territory.
  • What: A dual-DC EVPN/VXLAN fabric, ~40 Arista switches, automated from day one with AVD, Git and GitLab CI. The real work: extracting a coherent service model from a network that had no source of truth, discovering vendor-provided data models (AVD's) didn't fit their operational requirements, and building operator tooling (a CLI editor, validator, and search) so junior engineers could actually use the SOT. One year on, the ops team uses it daily; the biggest shift was in how they think about configuration, not speed.
  • How: Two layers: a CRA service SOT capturing service intent, and a translator to the AVD data model — service identity is global while VLAN/VNI mapping is POD-local, which forced the separate abstraction. Day-2 pipeline: edit → commit → MR → validate → translate → build → deploy, with avd-editor/avd-validator/avd-finder as operator-facing tools.
  • Where applicable: Arista/AVD-specific implementation at small-mid scale (40 switches, 2 DCs). The core lesson — service intent needs its own abstraction above the vendor model — generalizes to any fabric program.

items.title: Automating firewall rule deployment in a highly regulated environment
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

João Soares · Ørsted (per talk content)

  • Why: The strongest network-security item in the program: policy-as-code firewall automation with hard production numbers, in a highly regulated energy company.
  • What: DRAGØN, Ørsted's self-service firewall platform: internal customers define, validate and deploy their own rules via a request form or full GitOps workflow, with no firewall team involvement. Results as of 2026: 40+ teams, 150+ users, 3,500+ successful deployments, 3,000+ rejected-by-validation attempts, automated requests 0% → 80%, human-handled lead time down 88% — and total request volume up ~250%, exposing the hidden cost of the old slow process.
  • How: Security principles were moved out of SharePoint/Word/gut-feeling into policy-as-code: custom Nautobot models abstracting business/security concepts, related to real network constructs, connected by policy, exposed to humans via GUI and machines via API. Validation runs automatically against those policies; security is pulled in automatically when a rule requires it; Terraform deploys to the firewall management platform and Ansible commits to the firewalls. Compliant-by-design, fully versioned and revertable.
  • Where applicable: Regulated-enterprise specific (Danish critical energy infrastructure), but the pattern — security policy as queryable models rather than documents, plus treating the automation as a real product with versioning/changelog/support — transfers to any security-governed org.

items.title: Migrating the GÉANT Network to a new vendor
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Simone Spinelli · GÉANT (per talk content)

  • Why: A two-year, zero-major-disruption Juniper → Nokia migration of a pan-European IP/MPLS WAN at 800G — physical backbone and interconnection work at continental scale, exactly this PM's core.
  • What: GÉANT (31 PoPs, 44 nodes, >1,000 services: BGP-based L3, L2 circuits, directly attached servers) migrated to Nokia 7750-SR (SR-OS, not SR-Linux) between June 2024 and February 2026, while simultaneously building the in-house GÉANT Automation Platform (GAP) on open-source Workflow Orchestrator and Ansible.
  • How: Top-down modeling: every config line exists because it belongs to the node or to a service; one network construct = one Ansible role, with lifecycle management embedded. Peering is modeled org-centrically with lifecycle states (provisioned/active/disabled), covering IX peering, private peering, and upstreams. Concrete migration example: moving an IX port where GAP finds all peers, Moodi starts monitoring, Ansible generates config, operator confirms — AMS-IX with ~120 peers took 30 minutes.
  • Where applicable: GÉANT/NREN scale, but WFO is a genuinely open, joinable community (SURF, ESnet as partners; public money, public code). The "design as the primary source of truth" and per-construct role patterns transfer to any multi-vendor WAN.

items.title: Modernizing Workflows as Old as the Railways: Operationalizing Network Automation
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Leo Fleskes · Network Automation Architect — DB Systel GmbH (with Gerasimos Tzakis, Network to Code)

  • Why: The best data-quality war story in the program — two years of IPAM/inventory cleanup before any automation was possible at a 2,500+-router railway WAN. IPAM data hygiene is directly in this PM's wheelhouse.
  • What: Building a Single Source of Truth uncovered the brownfield mess: empty locations, "Düsseldorf" vs "Dusseldorf", VRF mismatches, DNS misconfigurations, missing or mis-attributed prefixes. A dedicated cleanup team plus daily issue reports produced +25% documented IP addresses and, crucially, organizational momentum. A VPN rollout that took 70 minutes across four teams now takes 25 across one.
  • How: Stage-by-stage: SoR interaction through small Nautobot jobs (allocation 25 → 5 min), configuration through an NSO service fed by the Nautobot job (30 → 1 min), documentation still manual. Platform scaling follows Conway: weekly integration meetings, shared responsibility split between platform team and device-owner teams, PRs reviewed from both sides.
  • Where applicable: Deutsche Bahn-scale brownfield WAN; the sequencing (data first, MVP workflows, blameless cleanup culture) and the "give us a 'let's fix it' mentality" tactic transfer to any brownfield IPAM/SoT effort.

items.title: Lessons Learned Testing Network Automation Solutions
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Ivan Pepelnjak · ipSpace.net

  • Why: The most transferable engineering talk of the conference — the testing methodology behind netlab, plus a multi-vendor NOS bug catalog that anyone testing across platforms will hit.
  • What: ~100 transformation tests plus ~100 error tests comparing against YAML-stored expected results (diffs reviewed in PRs); 25+ integration suites, 250+ individual tests across ~30 device types, requiring 3,700+ lab instances and days of runtime. Hard lessons: testing distributed systems takes longer than planned and vendor implementations will surprise you.
  • How: Multi-platform testing is solved by not parsing show output on ~20 platforms — instead, FRRouting probe containers attached to the device under test run JSON show commands and validate protocol behavior indirectly. Tiered CI: pre-commit (linting, some tests) → push → PR (all transformations) → dedicated server (full integration before release).
  • Where applicable: Broadly applicable to anyone building or testing multi-vendor automation. The quirks list is directly useful: Junos advertising wide IS-IS metrics as 63, Aruba CX invalid VXLAN IP checksums, mostly-broken OSPF NSSA implementations, divergent EVPN/ARP defaults, unresolved VRRPv3 checksum and MPLS entropy-label disagreements.

items.title: How Workflow-Driven Automation Becomes Operable Under Air Gap & Compliance Constraints
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

Henry Ölsner · NTT Germany & Christian Miene · 50Hertz

  • Why: Automation under German critical-infrastructure rules where always-on connectivity is not a given — and the use-case list includes an 802.1X migration (the only identity-adjacent item in the whole program) and MPLS VRF WAN segmentation.
  • What: A transmission-system operator's journey from unmanaged Python scripts, regex parsing and undocumented cron jobs on a backup server to a platform (DINA) run by a 5-person team: 106,654 workflow executions and 719 sub-process executions, covering CMDB sync, 802.1X migration, MPLS VRF rollout, a DC self-service portal, and VM network provisioning across ~4,000 devices in 6 network zones.
  • How: The Workflow Definition Document (WDD) is the centerpiece: one formal, auditable contract per use case containing goal/KPI, BPMN workflow, UI design, data models, constraints, and external dependencies — reviewed by stakeholders on a fixed cadence. Platform principles: air-gapped by design, build once/deploy unchanged, develop without live-system access, workload distributed via Django + Celery.
  • Where applicable: Specific to air-gapped, compliance-heavy critical infrastructure (dependency wheels chains, no GitLab connectivity), but the WDD-as-contract pattern is a strong fit for any change-managed environment, regulated or not.

items.title: Practical Network Reliability Engineering
items.text:
Slides (PDF) Slides (PPTX) Recording

John Howard · Head of Network Infrastructure — Proton AG

  • Why: Four years of applying NRE (SLI/SLO discipline) to a real network, with outcomes: 10x capacity since 2021, -40% per-port cost, zero extra headcount, zero out-of-hours change windows.
